section_summary: This section contains intelligence reports and diplomatic records from September and October 1944 detailing internal political, economic, and military conditions in Japan and the postwar program of the Japanese Communist Party. It opens with a report from Yenan by Foreign Service Officer John S. Service recording a detailed interview with Japanese Communist leader Okano Susumu (Nosaka Sanzō) regarding the party's gradual, three-stage program for postwar democratization and the abolition of militarism. An administrative Department of State form documents the subsequent declassification review of Service's report, followed by an American Embassy Chungking report transmitting translations from the Yenan newspaper Jiefang Ribao that describe acute food shortages, severe rationing failures, widespread black market activity, extreme labor fatigue, and growing defeatist anxieties among Japanese leaders.

subfiles.about: A report by John S. Service detailing an interview in Yenan with Japanese Communist leader Okano Susumu regarding the party's three-stage program for the postwar democratization and political reorganization of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Service Officer John S. Service of the U.S. Army Observer Section reports from Yenan on a September 8, 1944 conversation with Okano Susumu (Nosaka Sanzō), representative of the Central Committee of the Japanese Communist Party. Okano sets forth a moderate three-stage program starting with forcing an end to the war, overthrowing militarist rule, establishing universal suffrage, empowering the Diet, forcing the retirement of the current Emperor, and placing monopoly capital under government control. In subsequent stages, remaining feudal elements would be liquidated, voluntary collective agriculture encouraged, and a gradual transition toward socialism pursued through peaceful and democratic means. Service observes striking similarities between Okano's strategy and Chinese Communist policy, suggesting that the United States consider sympathetic support for the party as a dependable anti-militaristic group.
subfiles.title: The Program of the Japanese Communist Party

subfiles.about: A Department of State Form DS-507 requesting the declassification of Chungking Despatch No. 3021 and John S. Service's Report No. 24 of September 8, 1944.
subfiles.summary: Form DS-507 reclassifies Service's 1944 report on the Japanese Communist Party's postwar program from Secret to Unclassified, action completed 1970.

subfiles.about: An American Embassy Chungking report transmitting and summarizing translations from the Yenan newspaper Jiefang Ribao describing deteriorating economic conditions, rationing breakdowns, and war weariness in wartime Japan.
subfiles.summary: Second Secretary of Embassy Carl H. Boehringer, with the approval of Ambassador Clarence E. Gauss, submits Report No. 105 transmitting translations prepared by the American Co-ordinated Translation Center in Chungking of articles from the July 12, 1944 supplement of the Yenan Chinese Communist newspaper Jiefang Ribao. The enclosed articles draw upon Japanese periodicals and official statements to portray severe declines in food and clothing rations, pervasive black market trafficking, and the creation of fictitious family members ('ghosts') to secure extra food. The report further documents extreme worker exhaustion caused by 15- to 16-hour workdays and 'excessive spiritualism', malnutrition among nursing mothers in rural areas, and growing defeatist sentiment and rumors prompted by the loss of the Marshall Islands, air raid threats, and the death of Admiral Mineichi Koga.
subfiles.title: Conditions in Japan Described by Chinese Communist Paper
